  location as the impact point. The playtester throws with its `shoot` tool, so this path is what gets tested.
- **Pulling, vortexes, magnets**: in a `runTaskTimer` every tick, for each `LivingEntity` in range (skip spectators), set
  `velocity = toCenter.normalize().multiply(pull)` plus a sideways `new Vector(-dz, 0, dx).normalize().multiply(swirl)` for a spiral.
  Ground friction eats sideways velocity, so add a small upward part (0.08 to 0.2) to keep mobs moving. Mobs inside about
  1.5 blocks of the center should orbit or hover, not be pulled further. Log how many entities each pulse moved.
- **Explosions**: `world.createExplosion(sourceEntity, loc, power, setFire, breakBlocks)`. The blast's own knockback is weak
  and random; for a guaranteed launch, set each nearby entity's velocity one tick later (`runTask`), and log the count.
- **Spectacle**: the user watches through a real Minecraft client, so effects should be visible from 8 blocks away. Use
  plenty of particles (`world.spawnParticle(Particle.REVERSE_PORTAL, loc, 40, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.05)`; good ones are `PORTAL`,
  `REVERSE_PORTAL`, `DRAGON_BREATH`, `SQUID_INK`, `END_ROD`, `SONIC_BOOM`, `FLASH`, `EXPLOSION_EMITTER`, `DUST` with a
  `DustOptions`), rings and spirals computed with sin/cos around a center, and sounds (`world.playSound(loc, Sound.ENTITY_WARDEN_SONIC_BOOM, 2f, 0.6f)`).
  Lightning without fire or damage: `world.strikeLightningEffect(loc)`.

Now I'm designing the Play feature's backend logic, setting up a client that launches a local game server, tracking play state through stages like launching, joining, and live, and handling server startup errors before attempting to connect the player.

I'm also weighing gamemode options for the presenter — survival with resistance and saturation effects to keep boss mods and damage behavior realistic, versus creative for safer camera flying, ultimately leaning toward survival plus buffs while opping the player so they retain command flexibility.

For setup, I'll teleport the player near the arena facing the summon area and run the mod's testPlan setup commands with execute-as substitution for the real player instead of the bot, which should spawn mobs and items as intended even if some commands also clear inventory or reposition things slightly. I also need to make sure the resource pack server entry gets written into the correct game directory for the quickplay client, and the game window itself should launch normally at default size without being minimized, letting the presenter use fullscreen if needed.

On deploy or reset, I need the play client to disconnect too since the server restarts, so I'll stop it alongside the camera and track a `playWanted` flag — if the player was active before reboot, it auto-relaunches after the server comes back up, while a manual game stop clears that flag. For capture, I realize both the camera and player windows share identical titles, so I need another way to distinguish their HWNDs, likely by having the parking script report back the camera's window handle explicitly since the player window stays unparked.

For capturing the camera specifically, I'll have the park script spawn PowerShell to parse out the HWND and store it on the client, then match the desktopCapturer source by that HWND rather than title when available, falling back to title-based matching when the camera window is shown unparked. I also need to account for the Minecraft window's title being empty while loading, since the park script needs to wait until the title populates before locking onto the correct HWND for the GLFW window that persists afterward.

For the UI side, I'm thinking the "Play" button should trigger a studio-level handler that ensures the mod is loaded then calls into the game module to start play, passing along the setup commands from the mod's testPlan rather than having the game module depend on studio directly.

But studio/index.cjs currently has uncommitted changes from the marketplace work in progress, which complicates adding to it cleanly — simpler to keep the play logic self-contained in game/index.cjs, with 'game:play' accepting setup passed straight from the renderer.

For the player name, I'll use an env variable BENANA_PLAYER_NAME falling back to 'Player', and mention it can be customized for a demo. I'll also leave the nearby_entities bot tool as-is, excluding only the camera, since it's fine for the presenter to be visible during playtests.

I need to track each watched entity's height gain and proximity to the eventual impact point, so I'll store position samples every tick and compute the closest distance to the landing spot afterward.

The current loop ends 15 ticks after all projectiles settle, which won't capture lingering effects like black holes or poison clouds, so I'm adding a `watchTicks` parameter (default 0, max 300) that extends observation after landing. I'm also updating the sampling logic to track max height using the entity's position each tick.

For impact distance, I'll compute horizontal distance from each entity's position to the nearest projectile impact point, reporting start, closest, and end distances since horizontal matters more for lift effects. Then I need to update the MCP shoot tool schema and prompt documentation to mention the new watchTicks parameter.

Since players are excluded, maybe the bot itself fell into the crater, or the demo agent moved it somewhere that caused the camera to reframe oddly—perhaps looking upward from inside the crater where the ground level sits below the surrounding terrain.

Actually, I'm wondering if the explosion's knockback launched the bot airborne despite the exclusion, since the bot might still count as a blast-affected entity due to its resistance buff; if it got thrown high, the reframed camera position would end up sitting well above the terrain, looking down or outward across open sky.

The fix is to clamp the camera to a fixed arena floor height rather than deriving it from the bot's possibly displaced position, since the arena stays at the same elevation. I'm planning to rewrite frameCamera so it always uses the fixed arena floor y-value for the focus and shot coordinates, with a fixed offset for shot position and facing direction, though I still need to account for the bot's actual yaw/facing rather than assuming it always faces south after reset.

# Cloudflare API token for Artifacts (intent/harness repos, forks)
CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN=
# Cloudflare account id (optional; derived from token otherwise)
CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID=
# Artifacts namespace (default benana-dev)
ARTIFACTS_NAMESPACE=
# GitHub token (optional; falls back to `gh auth token`)
GITHUB_TOKEN=
# Neatlogs service-account API key for linked execution evidence
NEATLOGS_API_KEY=
# Neatlogs project id
NEATLOGS_PROJECT_ID=
# Neatlogs region, e.g. eu (optional)
NEATLOGS_REGION=
# Neatlogs dashboard link for one trace, with {traceId} (and optionally {projectId}) placeholders,
# e.g. copied from a trace page in the browser. Without it, "Open in Neatlogs" opens the dashboard.
NEATLOGS_TRACE_URL=
# Neatlogs project key for trace ingestion. Mod Studio installs @neatlogs/claude-code hooks
# into each generated mod repo with this key (falls back to NEATLOGS_API_KEY).
NEATLOGS_INGEST_KEY=
# Local data directory (default ~/.benana)
BENANA_DATA_DIR=

game.status()
// { server: 'stopped'|'starting'|'running'|'error', bot: 'offline'|'connecting'|'online',
//   viewerUrl: string|null, controlUrl: string|null, version: '1.21.4', mock: boolean, error: string|null,
//   deployed: { plugin, jar?, at? }|null,   // the studio mod on the server
//   deploying: string|null,                // jar name while a swap is in progress
//   camera: 'off'|'launching'|'joining'|'live'|'error', cameraEnabled: boolean, cameraError: string|null }

await game.start(emit)            // download/prepare Paper if needed, start the server, connect the bot, start the viewer
await game.stop()
await game.deployPlugin({ jarPath, packPath?, emit })
// Removes previously deployed studio jars, copies jarPath, restarts, waits for the bot.
// packPath is the mod's resource pack zip (target/<Name>-pack.zip); the server offers it to every player who joins,
// served from the control API at GET /pack.zip. A deploy without packPath removes the previous mod's pack.
// Deploys are queued, so a manual switch (IPC `studio:load { id }`) never overlaps a pipeline deploy.
// Every deploy wipes the saved world, so each mod starts on untouched terrain.
// -> { loaded: boolean, plugin: string|null, errors: string[], logTail: string[] }
await game.resetWorld({ emit })     // wipes the world and restarts with the same mod installed (queued with deploys; IPC `studio:reset-world`)
await game.runCommand('time set day')   // -> console output string

game.mcpConfig({ runId, verdictFile, testPlanFile })   // -> object to write as the Claude `--mcp-config` file
game.playtesterTools                                    // -> string[] for Claude `--allowedTools`
game.playtestPrompt(testPlan)                           // -> prompt for the playtester session
game.demoPrompt(mod) / game.demoTools                // showcase session behind the "Run mod" button (IPC `studio:demo { id }`); no verdict
game.readVerdict(verdictFile, testPlan)                 // -> verdict (see above); unreported plan checks count as blocked
game.mockVerdict(testPlan, attempt)                     // mock only: attempt 1 fails the first check, attempt 2+ passes
```

**Who runs the playtester:** B's pipeline spawns the playtester as a normal Claude Code run (`claude -p --output-format stream-json --mcp-config <file> --allowedTools <playtesterTools>`) with `playtestPrompt(testPlan)`. That way Neatlogs traces it like every other session. In mock mode, B skips the session and uses `mockVerdict`.

**Events** (main → renderer through `emit`):

- `game:status`: the status object above.
- `game:log`: `{ line, level: 'info'|'warn'|'error', at }`, server console lines.
- `game:action`: `{ tool, args, result?, at }`, each MCP tool call the bot performs, for the GamePane overlay.

**IPC** (registered by `game.handlers(emit)`): `game:status`, `game:start`, `game:stop`, `game:command { command }`, `game:camera { on }`.

**Real Minecraft camera** (`electron/lib/game/client.cjs`): after each boot, Benana launches a vanilla 1.21.4 client (downloaded from Mojang into `~/.benana/game/client` on first use) that joins as the offline player `Camera`, accepts the mod's resource pack, and is put in spectator mode behind the bot. On Windows its window is made frameless and parked off-screen. `main.cjs` captures that window through `getDisplayMedia`, and the live view shows it as the "Minecraft" source, with "Bot view" still showing the prismarine viewer. The bot and its MCP tools are unchanged: the camera only watches, `nearby_entities` leaves it out, and the plugin template tells builders to ignore spectators. Every deploy or reset relaunches the client, because vanilla cannot reconnect by itself. `BENANA_CAMERA=0` turns it off by default, and `BENANA_CAMERA_WINDOW=show` keeps the window on screen.

Runtime facts: the bot (`BenanaBot`) and viewer run in a child process under **system Node 22+**, because Mineflayer doesn't run on Electron 33's Node 20. A plugin swap takes about 16 seconds because it restarts the server. The world is a superflat at y=64, and the viewer is at `http://127.0.0.1:3007`.

This stdio MCP server forwards calls to the bot's local control API (`BENANA_GAME_URL`). The bot lives in the Electron main process, so the viewer and connection survive between sessions. Env: `BENANA_GAME_URL`, `BENANA_VERDICT_FILE`, `BENANA_TEST_PLAN`, `BENANA_RUN_ID`.
```

-Describe a Minecraft mod in one sentence. Benana writes it as a Paper plugin, starts a Minecraft server inside the app, and sends an AI player in to test it. When the playtest fails, a fixer agent reads the in-game evidence, patches the plugin, and the AI player tests it again.
-![Benana Mod Studio: the agent's report on the left, the live game, server log, Neatlogs traces and Entire checkpoints on the right](docs/images/build.png)
-> "A golden sword that launches any mob it hits into the sky with particles, with a 3 second cooldown."

-Type an idea, or pick one of the examples, and press Enter. You never open an IDE, a server console, or the game client. Lessons the fixer has learned from earlier mods are shown under the examples and passed to every new build.
-![The New mod composer with example ideas and the lessons the fixer has learned so far](docs/images/new-mod.png)
-1. **Spec agent** (Claude Opus) turns the sentence into behavior rules and an in-game **test plan** with measurable expectations, for example "the husk's upward velocity exceeds 0.8 blocks/tick".
-2. **Builder** (Claude Code, Opus) implements the plugin in its own git repository created from `templates/paper-plugin`, and Maven builds it.
-3. **Deploy**: Benana restarts its local Paper 1.21.4 server with the new jar, which takes about 16 seconds.

-4. **Playtester** (Claude Code, Sonnet) controls `BenanaBot`, a real player, through the `minecraft` MCP tools: equip, attack, use items, and track an entity's velocity tick by tick. It reports pass, fail, or blocked for each check, with the measurements as evidence.

-5. **Fixer** (Claude Code, Opus) receives the verdict, server stack traces, the mod's Entire checkpoint history, and the Neatlogs trace of the failed playtest. It fixes the root cause, writes down a **lesson**, and the loop runs again (up to 3 attempts).
-## Watch the AI player test it

-The live view embeds the game from BenanaBot's camera, so you see the playtest as it happens: the bot gets the item, spawns a target, and uses the mod on it. The server log streams next to it, so plugin errors are visible as they happen.
-![Three frames from BenanaBot's first-person view as it fights husks in the test arena](docs/images/live-view.png)
-## When a playtest fails, it fixes itself
-A failed check is not the end of the run. Every attempt keeps the measured evidence, the agent sessions behind it, and the fixer's lesson.

-The **Mods** page below shows ArrowTracer, a real run that needed three attempts. The request was "can't see the arrows being shot". The first build reported the arrow's landing spot 1.3 blocks from the shooter instead of 7 to 9. The fixer traced the impact point along the arrow's velocity and wrote that down as a lesson. The second playtest still failed. On the third attempt the fixer worked out that the plugin was right: the husk had walked up to the bot before the shot. It fixed the test target by giving it NoAI, and all four checks passed. Total cost: $1.32.
-![The Mods page: ArrowTracer's spec and its attempt timeline, with failed attempts, evidence and the fixer's lesson](docs/images/mods.png)

-Every builder, playtester, and fixer session is traced through `@neatlogs/claude-code` hooks installed into each mod repository. The **Neatlogs** page lists all sessions across all mods. Opening one shows its cost, tokens, the failure it was handed, each tool call, and its final output. The fixer reads the failed playtest's trace before it changes any code.
-![The Neatlogs page with the ArrowTracer fixer session open: duration, tokens, cost, the attempt 2 failure it received, and its 7 steps](docs/images/neatlogs-trace.png)
-## Every commit is tied to its session (Entire)

-Each agent commit in a mod repository carries an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer that links the code to the session that wrote it. The **Entire** page shows the commit history per mod: builder, playtest, and fixer commits in order, with the checkpoint that produced each one. The fixer gets this history as context.
-![The Entire page: ArrowTracer's six commits, alternating fixer attempts and playtests, each linked to a checkpoint](docs/images/entire.png)
-The **Insights** page tracks build outcomes, pass rate, first-try passes, and spend broken down by agent role and model.
-![The Insights page: mods built, pass rate, agent sessions, total spend, build activity and spend by agent role](docs/images/insights.png)
-- **Entire** checkpoints every attempt (see above). This repository has Entire enabled too.

-Track A (game) and Track B (studio) depend only on what this file defines. Change it only with both people agreeing, and update the mock in `electron/lib/game/index.cjs` in the same commit.
-The spec agent (B) writes it and the playtester (A) reads it.
-  "summary": "Hitting a mob with a golden sword launches it upward with particles. 3 second cooldown per player.",
-      "title": "Hitting a mob with a golden sword launches it upward",
-      "steps": "Equip golden_sword and attack the nearest zombie once.",
-      "expect": "The zombie's upward velocity exceeds 0.8 blocks/tick within 5 ticks of the hit."
-      "title": "A second hit within 3 seconds does not launch",
-      "steps": "Summon another zombie, hit it within 1 second of the first launch.",
-      "expect": "The second zombie's upward velocity stays below 0.5 blocks/tick."
-- `setup` entries are server console commands without a leading `/`. `@bot` is replaced with the bot's username, and the commands run as the bot so that `^`/`~` coordinates are relative to it.
-- `expect` must describe something the playtester tools can observe: entity position or velocity, inventory, chat, server log, health.

-- Don't summon mobs with `NoAI:1b`: they ignore velocity and knockback, so movement checks always fail. Prefer husks to zombies because zombies burn in daylight. Add `PersistenceRequired:1b` so mobs don't despawn.

-- Measured on the `fixtures/launch-sword` plugin: the correct build gives a max upward velocity of **1.6** (the mob rises about 13 blocks). The buggy build, where vanilla knockback overwrites the launch, gives **0.4**. Thresholds around 0.8 separate the two cleanly.
-The `minecraft` MCP server (A) writes it from the playtester's `report_check` and `finish` calls. The pipeline (B) reads it with `game.readVerdict(file)`.
-  "summary": "Zombie took damage but did not rise.",
-      "suspectedCause": "Velocity applied before the damage event resets it, or the event handler isn't registered."
-  "serverErrors": [{ "at": 1760140000000, "message": "Could not pass event EntityDamageByEntityEvent to LaunchSword", "stack": "..." }]
-- `status` is one of `pass`, `fail` or `blocked`. `blocked` means the playtester couldn't run the check, for example because the bot died or the plugin didn't load.
-- `passed` is `finished && every check passed && serverErrors is empty`.

-- Every check id in the test plan must appear. `finish` refuses once if any are unreported, then records the rest as `blocked`; `readVerdict(file, testPlan)` also fills unreported checks in as `blocked`, so a partial playtest never passes.
-- If the file is missing or the session never called `finish`, `readVerdict` returns `{ finished: false, passed: false, error }`. That never counts as a pass.
-//   viewerUrl: string|null, controlUrl: string|null, version: '1.21.4', mock: boolean, error: string|null,
-//   deployed: { plugin, jar?, at? }|null,   // the studio mod on the server
-//   deploying: string|null,                // jar name while a swap is in progress
-await game.start(emit)            // download/prepare Paper if needed, start the server, connect the bot, start the viewer
-// Removes previously deployed studio jars, copies jarPath, restarts, waits for the bot.
-// packPath is the mod's resource pack zip (target/<Name>-pack.zip); the server offers it to every player who joins,
-// served from the control API at GET /pack.zip. A deploy without packPath removes the previous mod's pack.
-// Deploys are queued, so a manual switch (IPC `studio:load { id }`) never overlaps a pipeline deploy.
-// Every deploy wipes the saved world, so each mod starts on untouched terrain.
-// -> { loaded: boolean, plugin: string|null, errors: string[], logTail: string[] }
-await game.resetWorld({ emit })     // wipes the world and restarts with the same mod installed (queued with deploys; IPC `studio:reset-world`)
-await game.runCommand('time set day')   // -> console output string
-game.mcpConfig({ runId, verdictFile, testPlanFile })   // -> object to write as the Claude `--mcp-config` file
-game.demoPrompt(mod) / game.demoTools                // showcase session behind the "Run mod" button (IPC `studio:demo { id }`); no verdict
-game.readVerdict(verdictFile, testPlan)                 // -> verdict (see above); unreported plan checks count as blocked
-game.mockVerdict(testPlan, attempt)                     // mock only: attempt 1 fails the first check, attempt 2+ passes

-**Who runs the playtester:** B's pipeline spawns the playtester as a normal Claude Code run (`claude -p --output-format stream-json --mcp-config <file> --allowedTools <playtesterTools>`) with `playtestPrompt(testPlan)`. That way Neatlogs traces it like every other session. In mock mode, B skips the session and uses `mockVerdict`.
-- `game:log`: `{ line, level: 'info'|'warn'|'error', at }`, server console lines.
-- `game:action`: `{ tool, args, result?, at }`, each MCP tool call the bot performs, for the GamePane overlay.

-**Real Minecraft camera** (`electron/lib/game/client.cjs`): after each boot, Benana launches a vanilla 1.21.4 client (downloaded from Mojang into `~/.benana/game/client` on first use) that joins as the offline player `Camera`, accepts the mod's resource pack, and is put in spectator mode behind the bot. On Windows its window is made frameless and parked off-screen. `main.cjs` captures that window through `getDisplayMedia`, and the live view shows it as the "Minecraft" source, with "Bot view" still showing the prismarine viewer. The bot and its MCP tools are unchanged: the camera only watches, `nearby_entities` leaves it out, and the plugin template tells builders to ignore spectators. Every deploy or reset relaunches the client, because vanilla cannot reconnect by itself. `BENANA_CAMERA=0` turns it off by default, and `BENANA_CAMERA_WINDOW=show` keeps the window on screen.

-Runtime facts: the bot (`BenanaBot`) and viewer run in a child process under **system Node 22+**, because Mineflayer doesn't run on Electron 33's Node 20. A plugin swap takes about 16 seconds because it restarts the server. The world is a superflat at y=64, and the viewer is at `http://127.0.0.1:3007`.

-This stdio MCP server forwards calls to the bot's local control API (`BENANA_GAME_URL`). The bot lives in the Electron main process, so the viewer and connection survive between sessions. Env: `BENANA_GAME_URL`, `BENANA_VERDICT_FILE`, `BENANA_TEST_PLAN`, `BENANA_RUN_ID`.

-| `read_chat(sinceMs?)` | Recent chat, action bar and title text (with a `kind`) |
-| `server_log(sinceMs?, level?)` | Server console, including plugin stack traces |
-| `report_check({ id, status, expected, observed, evidence?, suspectedCause? })` | Record one check result |

-IPC is registered by `studio.handlers({ emit, log })`. B defines the channel names and the mod object. The renderer side lives in `src/components/studio/**`. `ModStudio` renders `<GamePane />` from `src/components/game/GamePane.jsx`. `GamePane` takes no required props and subscribes to `game:*` events itself.

-Per-mod data (B): `<dataDir>/mods/<slug>/` is the plugin's git repo (Entire is enabled here). `<dataDir>/studio/<modId>/attempt-<n>/` holds `test-plan.json`, `verdict.json`, `build.log` and `mcp.json`.
+Track A (game) and Track B (studio) depend only on what this file defines. Change it only with both people agreeing, and update the mock in `electron/lib/game/index.cjs` in the same commit.
+The spec agent (B) writes it and the playtester (A) reads it.
+  "summary": "Hitting a mob with a golden sword launches it upward with particles. 3 second cooldown per player.",
+      "title": "Hitting a mob with a golden sword launches it upward",
+      "steps": "Equip golden_sword and attack the nearest zombie once.",
+      "expect": "The zombie's upward velocity exceeds 0.8 blocks/tick within 5 ticks of the hit."
+      "title": "A second hit within 3 seconds does not launch",
+      "steps": "Summon another zombie, hit it within 1 second of the first launch.",
+      "expect": "The second zombie's upward velocity stays below 0.5 blocks/tick."
+- `setup` entries are server console commands without a leading `/`. `@bot` is replaced with the bot's username, and the commands run as the bot so that `^`/`~` coordinates are relative to it.
+- `expect` must describe something the playtester tools can observe: entity position or velocity, inventory, chat, server log, health.

+- Don't summon mobs with `NoAI:1b`: they ignore velocity and knockback, so movement checks always fail. Prefer husks to zombies because zombies burn in daylight. Add `PersistenceRequired:1b` so mobs don't despawn.

+- Measured on the `fixtures/launch-sword` plugin: the correct build gives a max upward velocity of **1.6** (the mob rises about 13 blocks). The buggy build, where vanilla knockback overwrites the launch, gives **0.4**. Thresholds around 0.8 separate the two cleanly.
+The `minecraft` MCP server (A) writes it from the playtester's `report_check` and `finish` calls. The pipeline (B) reads it with `game.readVerdict(file)`.
+  "summary": "Zombie took damage but did not rise.",
+      "suspectedCause": "Velocity applied before the damage event resets it, or the event handler isn't registered."
+  "serverErrors": [{ "at": 1760140000000, "message": "Could not pass event EntityDamageByEntityEvent to LaunchSword", "stack": "..." }]
+- `status` is one of `pass`, `fail` or `blocked`. `blocked` means the playtester couldn't run the check, for example because the bot died or the plugin didn't load.
+- `passed` is `finished && every check passed && serverErrors is empty`.

+- Every check id in the test plan must appear. `finish` refuses once if any are unreported, then records the rest as `blocked`; `readVerdict(file, testPlan)` also fills unreported checks in as `blocked`, so a partial playtest never passes.
+- If the file is missing or the session never called `finish`, `readVerdict` returns `{ finished: false, passed: false, error }`. That never counts as a pass.
+//   viewerUrl: string|null, controlUrl: string|null, version: '1.21.4', mock: boolean, error: string|null,
+//   deployed: { plugin, jar?, at? }|null,   // the studio mod on the server
+//   deploying: string|null,                // jar name while a swap is in progress
+//   cameraWindow: string|null,             // the camera's window handle, so the capture never picks the player's window
+await game.start(emit)            // download/prepare Paper if needed, start the server, connect the bot, start the viewer
+// Removes previously deployed studio jars, copies jarPath, restarts, waits for the bot.
+// packPath is the mod's resource pack zip (target/<Name>-pack.zip); the server offers it to every player who joins,
+// served from the control API at GET /pack.zip. A deploy without packPath removes the previous mod's pack.
+// Deploys are queued, so a manual switch (IPC `studio:load { id }`) never overlaps a pipeline deploy.
+// Every deploy wipes the saved world, so each mod starts on untouched terrain.
+// -> { loaded: boolean, plugin: string|null, errors: string[], logTail: string[] }
+await game.resetWorld({ emit })     // wipes the world and restarts with the same mod installed (queued with deploys; IPC `studio:reset-world`)
+await game.runCommand('time set day')   // -> console output string
+game.mcpConfig({ runId, verdictFile, testPlanFile })   // -> object to write as the Claude `--mcp-config` file
+game.demoPrompt(mod) / game.demoTools                // showcase session behind the "Run mod" button (IPC `studio:demo { id }`); no verdict
+game.readVerdict(verdictFile, testPlan)                 // -> verdict (see above); unreported plan checks count as blocked
+game.mockVerdict(testPlan, attempt)                     // mock only: attempt 1 fails the first check, attempt 2+ passes

+**Who runs the playtester:** B's pipeline spawns the playtester as a normal Claude Code run (`claude -p --output-format stream-json --mcp-config <file> --allowedTools <playtesterTools>`) with `playtestPrompt(testPlan)`. That way Neatlogs traces it like every other session. In mock mode, B skips the session and uses `mockVerdict`.
+- `game:log`: `{ line, level: 'info'|'warn'|'error', at }`, server console lines.
+- `game:action`: `{ tool, args, result?, at }`, each MCP tool call the bot performs, for the GamePane overlay.

+**Real Minecraft camera** (`electron/lib/game/client.cjs`): after each boot, Benana launches a vanilla 1.21.4 client (downloaded from Mojang into `~/.benana/game/client` on first use) that joins as the offline player `Camera`, accepts the mod's resource pack, and is put in spectator mode. It frames the bot from its right-hand side at the arena floor's height, looking a few blocks ahead, so whatever the bot hits, throws or summons up to about 12 blocks ahead is in the shot. On Windows its window is made frameless and parked off-screen. `main.cjs` captures that window through `getDisplayMedia`, and the live view shows it as the "Minecraft" source, with "Bot view" still showing the prismarine viewer. The bot and its MCP tools are unchanged: the camera only watches, `nearby_entities` leaves it out, and the plugin template tells builders to ignore spectators. Every deploy or reset relaunches the client, because vanilla cannot reconnect by itself. `BENANA_CAMERA=0` turns it off by default, and `BENANA_CAMERA_WINDOW=show` keeps the window on screen. The clients run under `javaw` on Windows, so no console window opens.

+**Play in Minecraft** (`game:play`): a second vanilla client in a normal window, for the user to play the loaded mod themselves. It joins as `BENANA_PLAYER_NAME` (default `Player`), is op, gets Resistance like the bot, and stands next to the bot in the camera's shot. `playKit(plan)` hands it every item the mod's test plan gives (each `give` in the setup and in the checks' `game_setup` lists, once per kind) plus husk spawn eggs, and suggests the plan's other plugin commands in chat. A deploy or reset reopens it on the new world. It has its own game directory (`~/.benana/game/client/play`), so its options are kept between sessions.

content.content:
# neatHack submission checklist

Submissions are open Mon Oct 12, 19:00–23:55 IST. Plan to submit by 21:00.

| Requirement | Evidence | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Agent capability (30%) | Demo video: prompt → spec → build → in-game playtest fails → fixer → retest passes. Mod repos in `~/.benana/mods/*` | Loop verified headless on 2026-10-11 (seeded run: fail → fix → pass in 3m16s) |
| neatlogs | Trace links or screenshots for builder, playtester, and fixer sessions. Session IDs are in `~/.benana/studio/<mod>/mod.json` | Waiting on keys in `.env` |
| Entire | `entire checkpoint list` in a mod repo. `Entire-Checkpoint` trailers on every agent commit. Entire enabled on this repo | Checkpoints recorded locally. Run `entire login` for shareable links |
| cfo.ai | Business plan covering pricing, costs, revenue, runway: [cfo-plan.md](cfo-plan.md) | Inputs drafted. Run it in cfo.ai and paste the result |
| Failure recovery | Attempt timeline: the failed attempt with its measured evidence, the fixer's lesson, and the passing retest | Working |
| Public commits during the event | `git log` on `Pratheek555/benana` | Pushing at each milestone |
| Build log on X (#neatHack) | Posts #1–#6 from [PLAN.md](PLAN.md) | |
| Demo video (20%) | 2–3 minutes, recorded Mon 15:00–19:00 | |

## Demo video script (about 2:30)

1. **0:00–0:15. Hook.** "This AI just built a Minecraft mod, played it, found its own bug, and fixed it." Show the passing checklist.
2. **0:15–0:35.** Type the hero prompt and click **Build and playtest**. Show the spec agent's test plan appearing.
3. **0:35–1:00.** The builder writes the plugin (speed up this part), then compiles and deploys while the server restarts.
4. **1:00–1:40.** The playtester in the 3D view: equips the sword and hits the husk while the overlay shows the measured velocity. The check turns red, with the observed velocity next to it.
5. **1:40–2:10.** The fixer: it reads the evidence, the Entire checkpoint context, and the Neatlogs trace, writes its lesson, and the husk flies 13 blocks up. Everything turns green.
6. **2:10–2:30.** Evidence: a Neatlogs trace, `entire checkpoint list`, the cfo.ai plan. "Lessons carry over: the next mod doesn't repeat the bug."

If the organic run doesn't fail on camera, use **Seeded bug (fallback)** and say on screen that it's seeded.

## Crazy mod: Black Hole Grenade (ready, real Minecraft client)

Built in the app on 2026-10-12 (chat `BlackHoleGrenade`, repo `~/.benana/mods/black-hole-grenade-okx3`). Both turns passed every check on the first attempt; $2.29 in total.

1. Prompt (5 min, 4/4 checks): *"Black Hole Grenade: a dark orb you throw like a snowball. Where it lands, a black hole opens for 5 seconds: a swirling vortex of purple and black particles that drags every mob within 12 blocks into a spiral around it and lifts them off the ground. Then it collapses with a huge explosion that flings every mob caught in it high into the sky. 8 second cooldown per player."*
   The playtester measured a husk pulled from 4.9 to 0.5 blocks off the impact point, then launched at 2.2 blocks/tick and 26 blocks high.
2. Follow-up in the same chat (8 min, 5/5 checks): *"Make it way crazier: while the black hole is open it rips chunks of the ground up, so blocks tear off the floor and spiral into the vortex along with the mobs, and when it collapses lightning strikes the center and the blast leaves a crater."* The log reads "ripped 40 blocks, crater 189 blocks".
3. **Run mod**: the live view is the real Minecraft client, filmed from the side, so the vortex, flying blocks, lightning and crater are all in the shot.
4. **Play in Minecraft**: a second real Minecraft window opens with you next to the bot, holding 3 grenades and husk eggs. Throw it yourself on camera. **Reset world** fills the crater back in, and your window rejoins.

Shot list: type prompt 1 → speed up the builder → playtest in the live view → green checks → send prompt 2 → Run mod → Play in Minecraft and throw one yourself. Use ArrowTracer's history (or the seeded run) for the fail → fix → pass beat.

The crazy mod is built and the demo works in a real Minecraft client. Neatlogs and the commit are blocked on you, though (details at the end).

## The mod: Black Hole Grenade
I typed it into Benana like a user would, then sent a "make it crazier" follow-up in the same chat. Both turns passed every check on the first attempt, about 13 minutes and $2.29 in total:
- **Turn 1 (5 min, 4/4 checks):** you throw a dark orb and a 5-second vortex opens. The AI player measured a husk pulled from 4.9 to 0.5 blocks off the impact point, then flung 26 blocks into the air when the vortex collapsed.
- **Turn 2 (8 min, 5/5 checks):** the vortex now rips the ground up into flying blocks, lightning strikes when it collapses, and the blast leaves a crater. The mod's log reads "ripped 40 blocks, crater 189 blocks".

It's loaded on a fresh world right now. Here's the walkthrough in the app's live view, which is the real client:

![Black hole vortex and collapse in the real client](C:\Users\prath\.t3\projects\benana\.audit\demo\vortex.png)

## Real Minecraft client
- **New "Play in Minecraft" button.** It opens a second real Minecraft window and puts you next to the bot, holding 3 grenades and 16 husk spawn eggs for targets. After Reset world the window rejoins and gets its items again. I checked the join and the items; I couldn't throw from that window myself, so that part is only tested through the bot.
- **Camera fixes:**
  - The camera now films from the side, so the vortex, debris and crater stay in frame. Before, it re-framed onto the bot and could end up pointing at the sky.
  - The particle/sound list no longer covers the picture.
  - Chat is hidden on the camera.
  - The empty Java console windows that opened with each client are gone.

![Play in Minecraft window with the grenade](C:\Users\prath\.t3\projects\benana\.audit\demo\desk1.png)

## Agent improvements
- **Mod template guide:** added how to build throwable items, vortex/pull effects, explosions and visible particle effects.
- **AI player measurements:** `shoot` can keep watching after impact (`watchTicks`) and reports how far each mob was pulled and how high it was lifted. The AI player used this in turn 2, which fixed the late measurement it had in turn 1.

63/63 tests pass and the renderer builds. The demo script with both prompts and a shot list is in `docs/hackathon/SUBMISSION.md`. I also updated the README, `CONTRACTS.md` and `.env.example`.

## Needs you
1. **Neatlogs isn't receiving any traces.** The ingest service rejects `NEATLOGS_INGEST_KEY` as an invalid key, so no agent session since about 07:08 UTC yesterday has a trace, including this mod's. Generate a new project key in Neatlogs, put it in `.env`, and restart from the app. The code side is fixed: agent sessions now send traces with that key, and the in-app Neatlogs panel can read again (it showed "Not configured" before).
2. **Nothing is committed.** Your checkout is mid-merge (the pull of origin/main, conflicts resolved but not concluded), and git refuses partial commits during a merge. Once you run `git commit` to finish the merge, I can commit my files. Should I push after that?

To enable debug-port control I restarted `npm run dev` from your terminal. The app now runs from a hidden process I started, with a debug port on localhost:9333 (dev mode only).

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   - The user asked me to "try building a crazy mod for our demo and keep it ready, iteratively finish the work necessary do anything necessary and improve the agent if need by." Later they said "we need real minecraft client demo."
   - Delivered so far: a crazy mod (BlackHoleGrenade) built and passing through Benana's own pipeline; a real Minecraft 1.21.4 client as the live view (spectator "Camera" framed from the side); a "Play in Minecraft" button that opens a second real client window for the user with the mod's items; agent improvements (shoot measures height gain and impact distance, watchTicks, template cookbook on throwables/vortex/explosions/particles); Neatlogs key-handling fix.
   - Standing rules: never push to main without explicit permission (commit locally, ask before pushing); never ask for secrets in chat; do not print secret values.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Electron 33 app (Mod Studio) with main process (electron/main.cjs), IPC via electron/preload.cjs (`window.benana.invoke`), renderer React (src/components/game/GamePane.jsx, Hud.jsx, game.css).
   - Game runtime: electron/lib/game/index.cjs (server, bot, camera, play, deploy, reset, demo, playtest prompts), host.cjs (Mineflayer bot in system Node 22+), server.cjs (Paper 1.21.4), client.cjs (vanilla client launcher).
   - Studio pipeline: electron/lib/studio/index.cjs (spec → builder → compile → deploy → playtest → fixer, up to 3 attempts; revision turns; bench; demo), prompts.cjs, claude.cjs (headless `claude -p` stream-json), repo.cjs.
   - MCP tools for the bot: electron/mcp-minecraft.cjs (shoot, track_entity, track_self, move, use_item, etc.).
   - Windows window capture: PowerShell P/Invoke (EnumWindows, SetWindowPos, GetWindowLong) to strip the frame and park the window off-screen; desktopCapturer + getDisplayMedia matching the window handle.
   - Paper 1.21.4 API: PlayerLaunchProjectileEvent, ThrowableProjectile.setItem, ItemStack.asOne, Particle (REVERSE_PORTAL, SQUID_INK, DRAGON_BREATH, SONIC_BOOM, FLASH…), Sound.ENTITY_WARDEN_SONIC_BOOM, World.strikeLightningEffect, createExplosion.
   - Neatlogs: read API (`/api/v1/public/traces?sessionId=`) needs a token; hook ingestion `https://ingest.neatlogs.com/v1/traces` with `x-api-key`; @neatlogs/claude-code v0.1.8 reads NEATLOGS_API_KEY env first, then ~/.config/neatlogs/config.json.
   - Dev tooling: BENANA_CDP_PORT=9333 enables remote-debugging on the dev app; `.audit/demo/cdp.mjs` (eval/invoke/click/type/shot) drives the app; `.audit/demo/watch.cjs` reads mod.json progress. Windows API window enumeration used for checks.
   - Tests: `node --test tests/` (63 passing); `npx vite build` passes.

3. Files and Code Sections:
   - electron/lib/game/client.cjs (modified)
     - Why: launches vanilla Minecraft clients (camera and player) and parks/captures the camera window.
     - Changes: `constructor({ name = NAME, game = 'game', hidden = true })`; `PLAYER` from BENANA_PLAYER_NAME; `park(pid, hide)` resolves `hwnd=<n>` via PowerShell stdout; `writeOptions(game, camera = true)` forces fov 0.25, chatVisibility 2, notificationDisplayTime 0.5 for the camera only; spawn uses `javaw` on win32 when resolvable; log written to `<game>/client.log`; `module.exports = { Client, NAME, PLAYER, TITLE, dir }`.
   - electron/lib/game/index.cjs (modified, large)
     - `const { Client, NAME: CAMERA, PLAYER } = require('./client.cjs');`
     - state adds `play: 'off', playError: null, player: PLAYER`; `status()` adds `cameraWindow: client.hwnd`.
     - `const player = new Client({ name: PLAYER, game: 'play', hidden: false });` `let playRun = 0; let playSetup = { commands: [], tries: [] };`

# neatHack submission checklist

Submissions are open Mon Oct 12, 19:00–23:55 IST. Plan to submit by 21:00.

| Requirement | Evidence | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Agent capability (30%) | Demo video: prompt → spec → build → in-game playtest fails → fixer → retest passes. Mod repos in `~/.benana/mods/*` | Loop verified headless on 2026-10-11 (seeded run: fail → fix → pass in 3m16s) |
| neatlogs | Trace links or screenshots for builder, playtester, and fixer sessions. Session IDs are in `~/.benana/studio/<mod>/mod.json` | Waiting on keys in `.env` |
| Entire | `entire checkpoint list` in a mod repo. `Entire-Checkpoint` trailers on every agent commit. Entire enabled on this repo | Checkpoints recorded locally. Run `entire login` for shareable links |
| cfo.ai | Business plan covering pricing, costs, revenue, runway: [cfo-plan.md](cfo-plan.md) | Inputs drafted. Run it in cfo.ai and paste the result |
| Failure recovery | Attempt timeline: the failed attempt with its measured evidence, the fixer's lesson, and the passing retest | Working |
| Public commits during the event | `git log` on `Pratheek555/benana` | Pushing at each milestone |
| Build log on X (#neatHack) | Posts #1–#6 from [PLAN.md](PLAN.md) | |
| Demo video (20%) | 2–3 minutes, recorded Mon 15:00–19:00 | |

## Demo video script (about 2:30)

1. **0:00–0:15. Hook.** "This AI just built a Minecraft mod, played it, found its own bug, and fixed it." Show the passing checklist.
2. **0:15–0:35.** Type the hero prompt and click **Build and playtest**. Show the spec agent's test plan appearing.
3. **0:35–1:00.** The builder writes the plugin (speed up this part), then compiles and deploys while the server restarts.
4. **1:00–1:40.** The playtester in the 3D view: equips the sword and hits the husk while the overlay shows the measured velocity. The check turns red, with the observed velocity next to it.
5. **1:40–2:10.** The fixer: it reads the evidence, the Entire checkpoint context, and the Neatlogs trace, writes its lesson, and the husk flies 13 blocks up. Everything turns green.
6. **2:10–2:30.** Evidence: a Neatlogs trace, `entire checkpoint list`, the cfo.ai plan. "Lessons carry over: the next mod doesn't repeat the bug."

If the organic run doesn't fail on camera, use **Seeded bug (fallback)** and say on screen that it's seeded.

## Crazy mod: Black Hole Grenade (ready, real Minecraft client)

Built in the app on 2026-10-12 (chat `BlackHoleGrenade`, repo `~/.benana/mods/black-hole-grenade-okx3`). Both turns passed every check on the first attempt; $2.29 in total.

1. Prompt (5 min, 4/4 checks): *"Black Hole Grenade: a dark orb you throw like a snowball. Where it lands, a black hole opens for 5 seconds: a swirling vortex of purple and black particles that drags every mob within 12 blocks into a spiral around it and lifts them off the ground. Then it collapses with a huge explosion that flings every mob caught in it high into the sky. 8 second cooldown per player."*
   The playtester measured a husk pulled from 4.9 to 0.5 blocks off the impact point, then launched at 2.2 blocks/tick and 26 blocks high.
2. Follow-up in the same chat (8 min, 5/5 checks): *"Make it way crazier: while the black hole is open it rips chunks of the ground up, so blocks tear off the floor and spiral into the vortex along with the mobs, and when it collapses lightning strikes the center and the blast leaves a crater."* The log reads "ripped 40 blocks, crater 189 blocks".
3. **Run mod**: the live view is the real Minecraft client, filmed from the side, so the vortex, flying blocks, lightning and crater are all in the shot.
4. **Play in Minecraft**: a second real Minecraft window opens with you next to the bot, holding 3 grenades and husk eggs. Throw it yourself on camera. **Reset world** fills the crater back in, and your window rejoins.

Shot list: type prompt 1 → speed up the builder → playtest in the live view → green checks → send prompt 2 → Run mod → Play in Minecraft and throw one yourself. Use ArrowTracer's history (or the seeded run) for the fail → fix → pass beat.

The `t3-code` MCP server provides app-owned orchestration. Treat these concepts distinctly:

- `t3_thread_launch` and `create_threads` create ordinary top-level T3 conversations. Use them only when the user explicitly asks for separate/new/top-level threads or conversations. Never use them merely because the user said "subagent" or requested parallel delegated work.

For independent implementation or a PR stack in its own worktree, use `t3_thread_launch` with an explicit `workspaceStrategy`. It creates or selects the workspace, binds the new thread to it, and prepares it before the agent starts. Put the task in `message`, not `prompt`:

- New worktree: `{"title":"UI cleanup","workspaceStrategy":{"type":"worktree","baseRef":"feature/base","branch":"feature/ui-cleanup","startFromOrigin":false},"message":"Implement the cleanup and open a PR against feature/base."}`
- Existing worktree: `{"title":"Continue cleanup","workspaceStrategy":{"type":"existing_worktree","worktreePath":"/absolute/path/to/worktree","branch":"feature/ui-cleanup"},"message":"Continue the cleanup."}`
- Project's main checkout: `workspaceStrategy:{"type":"root"}`. Omitting workspaceStrategy also selects root; it does not inherit the caller's worktree.

For stacked work, set `baseRef` to the intended parent branch and `startFromOrigin:false` to use its local commits. Use `startFromOrigin:true` when you intend to fetch and start from origin. Uncommitted edits are not copied. Use `t3_worktree_list` to discover existing checkout paths. Project, model selection, and modes inherit unless supplied; launch requires a full-access/default caller.

`t3_thread_launch` is the single-thread launch tool. Use `create_threads` only for a batch of threads intentionally sharing the caller's checkout: it always inherits the caller's project, branch, and worktree and has no workspace override. Asking an agent to run `git worktree add` or `cd` in its prompt does not update T3's thread binding. Select the workspace in the launch call instead. `t3_worktree_handoff` moves the calling thread, not another thread, and cannot move a thread already attached to a worktree.

`t3_thread_launch` has no idempotency key. Retain its returned threadId and inspect it with `t3_thread_read` / `t3_thread_wait`; preparation can still be running after acceptance. If a launch fails or its response is lost, inspect `t3_thread_list` before retrying, since a thread may already exist.

Tool names may include a harness-normalized MCP prefix, such as `mcp__t3_code__delegate_task`; the semantics are the same. Some harnesses attach optional MCP servers lazily: if an initial tool-catalog scan does not show T3 tools, do not conclude that cross-provider delegation is unavailable. Make one bounded direct attempt using the known T3 tool name on the next tool step. In Codex code mode, for example, call `tools.mcp__t3_code__orchestrator_capabilities({})` before reporting that the capability is absent. The reader sees the page above that reply, so don't announce or restate it; add only what it doesn't say.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

**Do not spawn agents unless the user asks.** Each spawn starts cold and re-derives context you already have — it's the expensive path on this plan. A task with "multiple angles," "thorough," or several parts is not a request to spawn; handle it inline with your own tools. Only use this tool when the user explicitly says to use a subagent, or names one of the available agent types.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

## When not to use

If the target is already known, use the direct tool: Read for a known path, the Grep tool for a specific symbol or string. Reserve this tool for open-ended questions that span the codebase, or tasks that match an available agent type.

## Usage notes

- Always include a short description summarizing what the agent will do
- When the agent is done, its final report is not visible to the user. To show the user the result, you should send a text message back to the user with a concise summary of the result.
- Trust but verify: an agent's summary describes what it intended to do, not necessarily what it did. When an agent writes or edits code, check the actual changes before reporting the work as done.
- Agents run in the background by default. When an agent runs in the background, you will be automatically notified when it completes — do NOT sleep, poll, or proactively check on its progress. Continue with other work or respond to the user instead.
- **Foreground vs background**: Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — e.g., a research agent whose finding gates the edit you're about to make. Otherwise let it run in the background (the default) — this includes fire-and-forget work, independent investigations, and anything where the user might hand you something else in the meantime. Wanting the result "next" is not enough on its own.
- **Don't race**: after launching a background agent, you know nothing about its results. Never fabricate or predict them in any format — not as prose, summary, or structured output. The completion notification arrives in a later turn; it is never something you write yourself. If the user asks before it lands, say the agent is still running — give status, not a guess.
- To continue a previously spawned agent, use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name as the `to` field — that resumes it with full context. A new Agent call starts a fresh agent with no memory of prior runs, so the prompt must be self-contained.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tool access are set in its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter, or the SDK `agents` option); the `model` parameter here overrides the definition for this one call.
- Clearly tell the agent whether you expect it to write code or just to do research (search, file reads, web fetches, etc.), since a fresh agent is not aware of the user's intent
- If the agent description mentions that it should be used proactively, then you should try your best to use it without the user having to ask for it first.
- If the user specifies that they want you to run agents "in parallel", you MUST send a single message with multiple Agent tool use content blocks. For example, if you need to launch both a build-validator agent and a test-runner agent in parallel, send a single message with both tool calls.
- With `isolation: "worktree"`, the worktree is automatically cleaned up if the agent makes no changes; otherwise the path and branch are returned in the result.

## Writing the prompt

Brief the agent like a smart colleague who just walked into the room — it hasn't seen this conversation, doesn't know what you've tried, doesn't understand why this task matters.
- Explain what you're trying to accomplish and why.
- Describe what you've already learned or ruled out.
- Give enough context about the surrounding problem that the agent can make judgment calls rather than just following a narrow instruction.
- If you need a short response, say so ("report in under 200 words").
- Lookups: hand over the exact command. Investigations: hand over the question — prescribed steps become dead weight when the premise is wrong.

Terse command-style prompts produce shallow, generic work.

**Never delegate understanding.** Don't write "based on your findings, fix the bug" or "based on the research, implement it." Those phrases push synthesis onto the agent instead of doing it yourself. Write prompts that prove you understood: include file paths, line numbers, what specifically to change.

Example usage:

<example>
user: "What's left on this branch before we can ship?"
assistant: <thinking>A survey question across git state, tests, and config. I'll delegate it and ask for a short report so the raw command output stays out of my context.</thinking>
Agent({
  description: "Branch ship-readiness audit",
  prompt: "Audit what's left before this branch can ship. Check: uncommitted changes, commits ahead of main, whether tests exist, whether the GrowthBook gate is wired up, whether CI-relevant files changed. Report a punch list — done vs. missing. Under 200 words."
})
assistant: Ship-readiness audit running in the background.
<commentary>
The prompt is self-contained: it states the goal, lists what to check, and caps the response length. The agent runs in the background (the default), so the turn ends here — nothing about its findings is known yet. The report arrives in a SEPARATE turn, as a completion notification from outside; it is never something you write yourself.
</commentary>
[later turn — notification arrives as user message]
assistant: Audit's back. Three blockers: no tests for the new prompt path, GrowthBook gate wired but not in build_flags.yaml, and one uncommitted file.
</example>

<example>
user: "so is the gate wired up or not"
<commentary>
User asks mid-wait. The audit was launched to answer exactly this, and it hasn't returned. Give status, not a fabricated result.
</commentary>
assistant: Still waiting on the audit — that's one of the things it's checking. Should land shortly.
</example>

<example>
user: "Can you get a second opinion on whether this migration is safe?"
assistant: <thinking>I'll ask the code-reviewer agent — it won't see my analysis, so it can give an independent read.</thinking>
Agent({
  description: "Independent migration review",
  subagent_type: "code-reviewer",
  prompt: "Review migration 0042_user_schema.sql for safety. Context: we're adding a NOT NULL column to a 50M-row table. Existing rows get a backfill default. I want a second opinion on whether the backfill approach is safe under concurrent writes — I've checked locking behavior but want independent verification. Report: is this safe, and if not, what specifically breaks?"
})
<commentary>
The agent starts with no context from this conversation, so the prompt briefs it: what to assess, the relevant background, and what form the answer should take.
</commentary>
</example>

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

A powerful search tool built on ripgrep

  Usage:
  - ALWAYS use Grep for search tasks. NEVER invoke `grep` or `rg` as a Bash command. The Grep tool has been optimized for correct permissions and access.

  - Output modes: "content" shows matching lines, "files_with_matches" shows only file paths (default), "count" shows match counts
  - Use Agent tool (if available) for open-ended searches requiring multiple rounds
  - Pattern syntax: Uses ripgrep (not grep) - literal braces need escaping (use `interface\{\}` to find `interface{}` in Go code)
  - Multiline matching: By default patterns match within single lines only. For cross-line patterns like `struct \{[\s\S]*?field`, use `multiline: true`

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000ms / 30 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms
